text_blocks.snippet: Shock is diagnosed based on signs of poor blood flow to the body (hypoperfusion) accompanied by low or falling blood pressure. It's a life-threatening condition requiring immediate treatment to restore adequate oxygen delivery to organs. The specific type of shock (cardiogenic, hypovolemic, distributive, obstructive) influences the diagnostic approach and treatment.
snippet_highlighted_words: based on signs of poor blood flow to the body (hypoperfusion) accompanied by low or falling blood pressure

list.title: Hypoperfusion:
list.snippet: This manifests as cool, clammy skin, pale or ashen skin, rapid breathing, rapid heart rate, and altered mental status.

list.title: Hypotension:
list.snippet: Low blood pressure is a common finding, often with a systolic blood pressure below 90 mm Hg.

list.title: Organ Dysfunction:
list.snippet: Reduced urine output (oliguria), confusion, and lactic acidosis can indicate organ damage.

list.title: History and Physical Exam:
list.snippet: A rapid assessment of the patient's airway, breathing, and circulation, along with a focused history (e.g., trauma, bleeding, infection) and physical examination is crucial.

list.title: Investigations:
list.snippet: Depending on the suspected cause, tests like blood pressure monitoring, electrocardiogram (ECG), chest X-ray, blood tests (including arterial blood gas), and echocardiogram (ultrasound of the heart) may be performed, according to the Mayo Clinic and Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Determining the type of shock:
list.snippet: A wide pulse pressure and warm extremities suggest high cardiac output (distributive shock), while a narrow pulse pressure and cool extremities suggest low cardiac output (cardiogenic or hypovolemic shock).

text_blocks.snippet: Specific Types of Shock and Diagnostic Considerations:

list.title: Cardiogenic Shock:
list.snippet: Caused by heart failure, diagnosed by signs of hypoperfusion, hypotension, and evidence of heart dysfunction on ECG or echocardiogram, according to the Mayo Clinic.

list.title: Hypovolemic Shock:
list.snippet: Caused by severe blood or fluid loss (e.g., hemorrhage, severe vomiting, diarrhea), diagnosed by signs of hypoperfusion, hypotension, and assessment of fluid volume status, says the Mayo Clinic.

list.title: Distributive Shock:
list.snippet: Caused by widespread vasodilation (e.g., sepsis, anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock), diagnosed by signs of hypoperfusion, hypotension, and assessment of the underlying cause (infection, allergic reaction, etc.), according to the Cleveland Clinic.

list.title: Obstructive Shock:
list.snippet: Caused by obstruction to blood flow (e.g., tension pneumothorax, cardiac tamponade), diagnosed by signs of hypoperfusion, hypotension, and signs of the underlying obstruction (e.g., distended neck veins, absent breath sounds).
Shock is a medical emergency requiring prompt diagnosis and treatment.
Delays in treatment can lead to organ damage and death, says AccessMedicine.
A high index of suspicion is needed for subtle or atypical presentations of shock, according to AccessMedicine.
